SENTINEL‑RAT

Watching rodents continuously, in the dark, without traps — and turning what the camera sees into an early signal of disease risk.

In the field

A camera that phones home

A Raspberry Pi in the enclosure, uploading over a mobile phone connection.

On the server

A model that can be retrained

In the lab

A dataset built ahead of the field

Species imagery gathered and filtered so the model has something to learn from.

Smart ENvironmental Tracking and INference for Early Zoonotic Disease Risk via Rodent Activity Tracking

The problem

Rodents are the largest zoonotic reservoir — and we watch them badly

  • Rodents carry more zoonotic pathogens than any other group of mammals — hantaviruses, Leptospira, Borrelia, and others.
  • Spillover into people is ecological, not an event. It follows rodent numbers, how active they are, rainfall and flooding, and how people use the land.
  • Leptospirosis is the clearest case: risk rises and falls with rodent abundance and environmental contamination.
  • Yet surveillance still works backwards from human cases. By the time it registers, transmission has already happened.

The shift we want: from counting sick people afterwards, to reading the ecological signal that comes first.

How rodents are counted today

Live trappingInvasive, labour‑intensive, only a snapshot
Footprint trackingHard to compare between sites
Direct observationDoes not scale; depends on the observer

All three give occasional data, at exactly the scale where a continuous signal is what matters.

Two places, one problem

Germany — rats, wood mice and voles; hantavirus and leptospirosis.
Sri Lanka — black rats dominant, shrews and bandicoot rats alongside; leptospirosis‑prone paddy and peri‑urban landscapes.

The technical gap

Camera-trap AI is solved for big animals. Rodents are a different problem.

Mature

Medium and large mammals

  • Models identify and count wildlife reliably in cluttered camera‑trap scenes
  • Satellite‑connected traps already send real‑time elephant alerts from remote Gabon
  • Pretrained models exist; the recipe is well understood
Open

Small mammals

  • Small, fast, and hidden — in burrows, vegetation, crop cover
  • Ordinary cameras fail exactly where rodents are active: night, shade, clutter
  • Existing rodent work is laboratory work, not field work
  • Thermal imaging is barely explored for this
  • Every group builds its own system from scratch

Gap 1 · Seeing
Combining an ordinary camera with a heat camera has not been tested on small mammals in the field.

Gap 2 · Meaning
Detections are not yet turned into the activity measures a public health office can act on.

Gap 3 · Reuse
No shared, adaptable system that another site can pick up and retrain.

What we built

One loop: the field feeds the model, the model goes back to the field

The point of the loop is that it closes. A site that sees different animals does not need different software — it needs its own images labelled, and the same machinery produces a detector for it.

In the field

A camera that works where there is no internet and nobody to visit it

It decides when to look

The camera watches a small, low‑resolution version of the scene and takes a full photograph only when enough of the picture changes. A quiet night costs almost nothing; a busy one is captured properly.

It can also be set to photograph on a fixed schedule instead — which is how we test whether motion triggering is missing anything.

Peak so far: about 1,000 images in a day from a single camera.

It never loses an image

Photographs queue up on the device and are sent oldest‑first. Each one is retried until the server confirms it arrived. If the connection is down for a day, nothing is lost — it simply catches up.

Each image travels with the time it was taken and how much movement triggered it, so months later you can still ask what the camera was reacting to.

Connections in the field are slow and unreliable by default. Designing for that first was the single best decision in the project.

It can be managed remotely

  • By text message — settings can be changed by SMS when there is no data connection at all. The device replies to confirm.
  • By dashboard — a web page showing signal strength, queue length and recent activity.
  • Software updates are collected by the device itself; nobody has to travel to the enclosure.

Hardware: Raspberry Pi, standard camera, a mobile‑network module, and a small heat sensor. All off the shelf.

On the server

Labelling is the bottleneck — so it lives one click from the data

How a detector gets better here

  • Open a page, get an unlabelled image. No exporting to another tool, no round trip. Draw a box, say what it is, submit.
  • An empty image is also an answer. Marking "nothing here" is what teaches the detector not to see rats in shadows.
  • Retraining is one action, and it runs on the same machine that holds the images.
  • A new detector only goes live if it scores better than the one in use. The previous version is kept, so going back is instant.

Why this matters more than the model architecture: every site will see different animals in different surroundings. The thing that transfers is not our detector — it is the machinery for producing theirs.

New: the heat map sits beside the photograph

The labelling tool now shows both at once, aligned to the same view. When an animal is in shadow in the photograph, the heat map settles the question — and the person drawing the box can see both before deciding.

This is how the examples later in this talk were labelled.

Where the effort actually goes

Collecting imagesAutomatic, continuous, essentially free
Labelling themHuman time. The whole constraint.
TrainingAbout an hour on one machine
It works

Four rats, one frame, in an enclosure at Heidelberg Zoo

Found by the retrained detector, minutes after the image arrived over the mobile network. Each animal is a few dozen pixels against straw, wood and equipment, under infrared light — the conditions the literature says ordinary camera traps handle badly. The scores, 0.49 to 0.68, say it another way: found, but not found confidently.

A working pipeline — not yet a working instrument
Accuracy of 0.74 from 129 boxes proves the loop closes: capture, send, label, train, deploy, detect, on real field data. It does not prove the detector works anywhere else.

Half the labelled images were deliberately marked empty. Teaching a detector what is not an animal turned out to matter as much as showing it what is.

Where it breaks

The failure modes are visible in the detector's own output

What you can see going wrong

  • The infrared lamp blows out whole frames. Nothing can be found in the white patch.
  • Animals far from the lens are missed. Too few pixels to be sure about.
  • Scores swing between 0.3 and 0.9 on frames that look the same to us.

What the picture cannot show you

  • One enclosure, one camera, one angle. Nothing here tests whether it travels.
  • Two categories: rat and person. That is not a wildlife survey.
  • Almost nothing is labelled. Labelling, not collecting, is what limits us.

Both problems — poor light and too few labels — are what the second camera channel was added to attack.

Since July 2026 · the second channel

Every photograph now arrives with a heat map

13,000+
Photographs since 1 July
11,600+
With a paired heat map

They looked broken, and they were not. Each heat map is stored as a number from 0 to 255 spread across a fixed 10–45 °C range. A cool enclosure occupies only about 20–26 °C of that, so every value landed in the bottom fifth and the image came out black. The sensor was fine; the way we drew it was not.

Fixed, and fixed everywhere

Heat maps are now converted back to degrees and drawn on a blue‑to‑white temperature scale — in the browser viewer, in the labelling tool, and in every image in this talk. It cost about forty lines of code and changed what the archive is worth.

What the heat map adds

An animal you would argue about becomes one you would not

Every box on this slide was drawn by a person, in the labelling tool, with both panels visible — not produced by the detector. These are ground truth, not results.

The honest half

Heat is a good hint about where. It is a poor answer to what.

Animal-to-background difference, by how warm the surroundings are

14 hand‑labelled animals. Each dot is one box.

The brightest thing is often the lamp. The camera's own infrared light reflecting off a basket is genuinely hot — and larger than any rat.

The two pictures are not simultaneous. They are taken one after the other, so a moving animal lands in slightly different places.

80 × 62 pixels. Enough to say something warm is there. Never enough to say which species.

In the lab

Building a training set before the field can supply one

Why screen automatically

Public archives are full of pictures that are the right species and completely the wrong thing — roadkill, skulls, specimens in drawers, trapped animals. A vision model rejects those at a scale no person could, and flags the doubtful ones for a human.

About 30 species, deliberately more than we need

Rats, mice and voles; shrews included on purpose because they are easy to confuse with rodents; and predators — snakes, buzzard, fox, badger. Central Europe and Sri Lanka in one list.

The caveat we keep in view

These are photographs people took deliberately, not camera‑trap frames. The angles and distances differ from what a camera looking down at a burrow sees. Whether that knowledge transfers is an open question, not an assumption.

In the lab · what we tested

Off-the-shelf models: none of them is the answer yet

The last bar is the good news. A shrew is not a rodent, and 13% is the model correctly declining to call it one. Above it the pattern is legible too: the rats that live alongside people score highest, the voles that live in fields score lowest.

Four candidates, same test set

A camera‑trap specialist Almost perfect at "an animal is here", but trained on beavers and elk — it struggles with animals this small.
A describe‑it‑in‑words model Good at animals in general; noticeably weaker when asked specifically for rodents.
A general object detector Weakest out of the box — but small, fast, and the one we can retrain.
A species‑matching model Fine at "animal", poor at species. Included as a baseline; behaved as advertised.

What we concluded

  • Retrain the small, fast one on our own images. Least glamorous, carries furthest.
  • Ask two questions, not one: first "is something here, and how sure am I?", then "what is it?" Uncertain cases go to a person instead of being guessed.
  • Species‑level naming may be out of reach until field data exists. Telling rats from mice is a legitimate interim goal.
Where this goes

Staged validation: enclosure → semi-natural site → Sri Lanka

Why a zoo first

Known animals, known conditions, safe access, and keepers who can tell you what you actually photographed. It lets camera placement, bandwidth, triggering and detector quality be tested one at a time — before ecological complexity is added on top.

Next · a semi-natural site

A purpose‑built plot at the zoo with vegetation, burrows and varied ground. Ecological complexity, still under control.

Then · Sri Lanka

Leptospirosis‑prone farmland and peri‑urban areas, with the University of Colombo and the Ministry of Health. Run alongside conventional trapping, so the two can be compared directly on what they detect, what they cost, and how much they disturb.

Cameras mount high and angle down at runs and burrow entrances — a geometry that keeps people's faces out of frame by construction.

Summary

The loop is closed and the second channel is live. Now it needs labels.

Working today
  • A camera in the enclosure, triggered by movement
  • Images uploaded over a mobile connection, never dropped
  • Managed remotely — by dashboard, and by text message
  • Photograph and heat map for over 11,600 captures
  • Labelling, retraining and a quality gate before anything goes live
  • A detector that finds rats in the dark
In progress
  • A training set assembled and screened in the lab
  • Around 30 species across two countries
  • Model comparison finished — retrain the small, fast detector
  • A two‑step design: is something there, then what is it
  • A dashboard turning detections into activity measures
What we need
  • Labelling time. Almost nothing collected since July is labelled yet. This is the single constraint.
  • More than one enclosure. One camera cannot train a wildlife detector.
  • A decision on heat. Keep it as a hint about where to look, or invest in a better sensor.
  • Confidence we can trust — evidence gathered across frames, not one score per picture.

This is not a rat detector that happens to have a pipeline around it. It is a pipeline that can be retrained into whatever detector a site needs — which is the part that travels from a Heidelberg enclosure to a paddy field in Sri Lanka.
